about.title: Sierra Madre Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: A workplace injury in a small city like Sierra Madre often gets complicated fast. Maybe you work for a contractor doing repairs near Lima Street, or you're injured while making deliveries along E Sierra Madre Boulevard. Your first path is usually workers' compensation through your employer, since California law generally makes that the exclusive remedy regardless of who was at fault. But that's not always the end of the story. If a subcontractor, property owner, equipment manufacturer, or another driver contributed to your injury, you may have a separate claim against that third party outside the workers' comp system. LawProactive doesn't practice law ourselves—we're a free service that connects injured workers in Sierra Madre with an independent attorney who can look at your specific situation, explain your options, and help you understand whether workers' comp, a third-party claim, or both apply to you.

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: California generally treats workers' comp as the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can still be held separately liable.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter Early On
items.desc: You typically have only 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and missing that window can jeopardize your ability to recover benefits.

items.title: Your Job Is Protected By Law
items.desc: Retaliation against you for reporting an injury or filing a claim is illegal in California, and an attorney can help you understand your rights if you feel pressured.

items.question: I was hurt driving for work near Sierra Madre Boulevard—does workers' comp cover that?
items.answer: Generally, yes, if you were injured while performing job duties, including driving on public roads like Sierra Madre Boulevard or Michillinda Avenue. However, if another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate third-party claim against them. An attorney can help sort out how both claims interact.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for my workplace injury?
items.answer: In most cases, California law makes workers' compensation your exclusive remedy against your employer, regardless of fault. That said, if a third party—like a contractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer—contributed to your injury, you may be able to pursue a separate claim against them.

items.question: How long do I have to act after a workplace injury in Sierra Madre?
items.answer: You should report the injury to your employer within 30 days to protect your workers' comp rights. If you also have a claim against a third party, California generally allows two years from the date of injury to file that separate lawsuit. Because these timelines run differently, it helps to get guidance early.
